new_statements.quote: 彝语中的每个音节都有声调。但各地的声调数量多少不等,一般有3-5个声调。彝语南部方言双柏话有高平、中平、低降三个声调。彝语除了有声调外,有些音节还带有表意重音或表情重音。重音是相连的音节中某个音节发音突出的现象,它出现在句子中,同时也出现在某些语言的单词中。如云南双柏彝语: do2'love33 “得了!”或“够了!”(看见异常情况时所发出来的自然感叹声或紧急呼声)凉山彝语 … mo33 “阿妈!”(遇到危险时的惊呼声)这类摹描自然声响的象声词和叹词,都带表意重音或表情重音。另外,彝语的表意重音有区别词汇意义和语法意义的作用。
new_statements.translation: Every syllable in Yi carries a tone, though the number of tones varies from place to place, generally 3-5. The Shuangbai speech of the Southern dialect of Yi has three tones: high level, mid level and low falling. Besides tone, in Yi some syllables also carry sense-marking stress (表意重音) or expressive stress (表情重音). Stress is the phenomenon in which one syllable among connected syllables is pronounced prominently; it occurs in sentences and, in some languages, also within words. E.g. Yunnan Shuangbai Yi do21 lo33 've33 'That will do!'/'Enough!' (a spontaneous exclamation or urgent cry on seeing something unusual); Liangshan Yi ... mo33 'Mother!' (a cry of alarm in danger) - onomatopoeic words and interjections of this kind all carry sense-marking or expressive stress. In addition, the sense-marking stress of Yi serves to distinguish lexical meaning and grammatical meaning.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Shuangbai (E-Xin) Nisu is described as a syllable-tone language (every syllable bears one of three tones, 55/33/21) with no positional word-stress rule; instead the author recognises a marked, sporadic 'sense-marking stress' and 'expressive stress' borne by particular syllables (interjections, onomatopoeia, and elsewhere as a lexically/grammatically contrastive feature). Where such stress falls within a word is not stated in the accessible text.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that interjections/onomatopoeia carry expressive or sense-marking stress and that sense-marking stress can distinguish lexical and grammatical meaning; no positional statement or exceptions visible.
new_statements.domain_note: The passage is framed for 'Yi' in general with the author's own Shuangbai Southern-Yi datapoint as the example (plus a Liangshan Yi example); stress is said to occur 'in sentences and also in words'. Only snippet-level access: a later, fuller treatment of 表意重音 in the Shuangbai description proper (e.g. on demonstratives or reduplication) could exist but did not surface in any snippet query (mine or the ache1244 second reader's).
new_statements.identity_note: Target languoid: Glottolog nort2718 'Northwestern Nisu' = ISO yiv 'Northern Nisu' = Chen et al.'s E-Xin (Eshan-Xinping) Yi = Yang 2009's NW Nisu (Eshan, Xinping, Yimen, Jiangchuan, Hongta, Tonghai, Jinning, Shuangbai; autonym Nasu(pho) in Eshan, Nishu/Nyiesu in Xinping). The quoted source, Li Shengfu 1996, describes 双柏话 (Shuangbai county Nisu), which Li himself labels '南部方言峨新土语' (E-Xin vernacular) and which Yang 2009 p.15 explicitly uses as her evidence for NW Nisu - hence nort2718. Caveat: Glottolog 5.1's sources.bib files Li 1996 under farn1234 [nsf] 'Far Northwestern Nisu' (apparently equating Yang's 'NW Nisu' with the ISO name 'Northwestern Nisu' = Yongping/Yunlong Nisu); by content (Shuangbai, E-Xin) the datapoint belongs with nort2718, but the catalog should record the Shuangbai datapoint explicitly. The statement itself is framed pan-Yi with Shuangbai examples.
